fields.Question: What is the OS abstraction for a running program with its own address space?
fields.Hint: It is the unit that fork() duplicates.
fields.Fact: OSTEP calls this one of the most fundamental abstractions an operating system provides to users.

fields.Text: Threads in the same process share the {{c1::address space}}, but each thread has its own {{c2::stack}} and registers.
fields.Extra: Shared memory makes communication between threads cheap but requires synchronization.
fields.Hint: Think about what one thread can see of another's variables.
fields.Fact: Because each thread has its own program counter, threads of one process can run different code at the same time.

fields.Question: Which Unix system call creates a new process by duplicating the caller?
fields.Hint: The caller and the new process both return from the same call.
fields.Fact: The child gets copies of the parent's file descriptors, which refer to the same open file descriptions.

fields.Question: What value does fork() return in the child process?
fields.Hint: The parent gets something more useful to identify the child.
fields.Fact: In the parent, fork() returns the child's PID, and on failure it returns -1 with no child created.

fields.Question: Which system call replaces the calling process's program with a new one?
fields.Hint: The library wraps it in several variants such as execl and execvp.
fields.Fact: On success execve() does not return, because the code that called it no longer exists in the process.

fields.Question: Which system call lets a parent block until one of its children changes state?
fields.Hint: Shells use it to know when a foreground command has finished.
fields.Fact: waitpid() can wait for a specific child and, with WNOHANG, return immediately if none has changed state.

fields.Text: A child that has terminated but has not yet been waited for by its parent is a {{c1::zombie}} process.
fields.Extra: The kernel keeps a minimal entry so the parent can still collect the exit status.
fields.Hint: It is neither alive nor fully gone.
fields.Fact: If a parent never reaps its children, zombies can fill the process table and block new process creation.

fields.Text: When a parent exits first, its {{c1::orphaned}} children are reparented to init (PID 1) or the nearest subreaper.
fields.Extra: The new parent reaps them when they exit.
fields.Hint: Think of a child that has lost its parent.
fields.Fact: Linux lets a process mark itself as a child subreaper with prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER).

fields.Question: What PID does the init process have on Unix-like systems?
fields.Hint: It is the first user space process the kernel starts.
fields.Fact: On Linux, if the init process of a PID namespace terminates, the kernel kills every other process in that namespace.

fields.Text: The kernel keeps each process's state, saved registers and resources in a {{c1::process control block}} (PCB).
fields.Extra: It is what the scheduler saves and restores on a context switch.
fields.Hint: Its abbreviation is three letters.
fields.Fact: OSTEP describes the PCB as the per-process data structure the OS uses to track each process.

fields.Question: What is the name of the Linux kernel structure that represents a process or thread?
fields.Hint: Linux calls schedulable entities tasks.
fields.Fact: Linux uses the same structure for processes and threads, because both are tasks to the scheduler.

fields.Text: In OSTEP's simple model, a process is {{c1::running}}, {{c2::ready}} or {{c3::blocked}}.
fields.Extra: A process waiting for I/O to complete cannot be scheduled until the I/O finishes.
fields.Hint: One state means it could run but is waiting for the CPU.
fields.Fact: Moving a process from ready to running is called scheduling it; moving it back is descheduling.

fields.Question: Which Linux system call creates new tasks with flags that control what they share with the caller?
fields.Hint: Both fork() and pthread_create() are built on top of it in glibc.
fields.Fact: Linux 5.3 added clone3(), which takes its arguments in a structure.

fields.Text: Linux creates threads with clone() using the {{c1::CLONE_VM}} flag so the new task shares the caller's memory.
fields.Extra: Other flags such as CLONE_FILES and CLONE_SIGHAND share descriptors and signal handlers.
fields.Hint: The flag name refers to virtual memory.
fields.Fact: Without CLONE_VM, the child runs in a separate copy of the caller's memory, as with fork().

fields.Text: fork() on Linux uses {{c1::copy-on-write}} pages, so memory is copied only when the parent or child writes to it.
fields.Extra: Until then both processes map the same physical pages read-only.
fields.Hint: The copy is deferred until a modification happens.
fields.Fact: This is why fork() followed quickly by exec() is cheap even for a large parent.

fields.Question: Which threading model maps many user threads onto a single kernel thread?
fields.Hint: A blocking system call in one thread can block them all.
fields.Fact: Pure user level thread libraries cannot run threads of one process on several CPUs at once.

fields.Question: Which threading model does the Linux NPTL implementation use?
fields.Hint: Each pthread is backed by its own kernel scheduling entity.
fields.Fact: NPTL replaced the older LinuxThreads implementation, which was also 1:1 but had many POSIX conformance gaps.

fields.Question: Which threading model multiplexes many user threads over a smaller or equal number of kernel threads?
fields.Hint: Goroutines in Go are scheduled in a similar way.
fields.Fact: This hybrid approach needs cooperation between the user scheduler and the kernel scheduler.

fields.Text: pthread_create() starts a thread and {{c1::pthread_join}}() waits for it to terminate.
fields.Extra: Joining also collects the thread's return value.
fields.Hint: It is the thread equivalent of waiting for a child process.
fields.Fact: A thread that is neither joined nor detached keeps some resources after it exits, similar to a zombie process.

fields.Text: pipe() returns two file descriptors: fd[0] is the {{c1::read}} end and fd[1] is the {{c2::write}} end.
fields.Extra: Data written to the pipe is buffered by the kernel until read.
fields.Hint: Remember: 0 is like standard input.
fields.Fact: Shells connect commands such as ls | wc by creating a pipe before forking both processes.

fields.Text: After fork(), parent and child descriptors refer to the same open file description, so they share the file {{c1::offset}}.
fields.Extra: A read by one moves the position seen by the other.
fields.Hint: It records where the next read or write happens.
fields.Fact: Opening the same file twice with open() creates separate descriptions with independent offsets.
fields.Source:
fork(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)
open(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html)

fields.Question: Which IPC mechanism gives a one-way byte stream between related processes, created by a call of the same name?
fields.Hint: Shells use it to connect commands.
fields.Fact: A named version created with mkfifo() lets unrelated processes use the same mechanism.

fields.Question: Which IPC mechanism lets processes map the same physical memory into their address spaces?
fields.Hint: It is the fastest IPC method once set up, but needs separate synchronization.
fields.Fact: POSIX shared memory objects live under /dev/shm on Linux.

fields.Hint: Each process has one, shown by ps.
fields.Fact: Linux's default pid_max is 32768, and it can be raised through /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max.

fields.Hint: Pipes, sockets and shared memory are examples.
fields.Fact: Unix domain sockets can pass open file descriptors between processes with SCM_RIGHTS.

fields.Text: A {{c1::context switch}} saves the registers of the currently running task and restores those of the next one.
fields.Extra: It is done by low level kernel code, often in assembly.
fields.Hint: It is how the kernel changes which task is on the CPU.
fields.Fact: Besides saving registers, a context switch can leave caches and the TLB cold for the next task.

fields.Question: Which scheduling policy runs jobs strictly in the order they arrive?
fields.Aliases:
FCFS
first come first served
first in first out
fields.Hint: It is the simplest policy and easy to implement.
fields.Fact: Its average turnaround time is poor when a long job arrives before short ones.

fields.Question: Which non-preemptive policy runs the job with the shortest total run time first?
fields.Hint: It needs to know job lengths in advance.
fields.Fact: If all jobs arrive at the same time, it is optimal for average turnaround time.

fields.Question: Which preemptive policy always runs the job with the least remaining time?
fields.Aliases:
shortest time-to-completion first
SRTF
shortest remaining time first
PSJF
fields.Hint: It is the preemptive version of a well known non-preemptive policy.
fields.Fact: OSTEP shows it is optimal for average turnaround time when jobs arrive at different times.

fields.Question: Which policy runs each job for a fixed time slice and then moves to the next in the queue?
fields.Hint: It is fair over short time scales.
fields.Fact: It gives good response time but is among the worst policies for turnaround time.

fields.Text: The {{c1::convoy effect}} is when short jobs queue behind a long running job, as under FIFO.
fields.Extra: It hurts average turnaround time.
fields.Hint: Picture cars stuck behind a slow truck.
fields.Fact: Preemptive policies such as STCF avoid it by letting short jobs run first.

fields.Text: In round robin, a shorter time slice improves {{c1::response time}} but increases context switch overhead.
fields.Extra: The slice must be long enough to amortize the cost of switching.
fields.Hint: It measures how soon a job first gets to run.
fields.Fact: OSTEP uses the term amortization for making the slice long enough that switch cost is a small fraction.

fields.Question: Which scheduler uses several priority queues and adjusts a job's priority based on its observed behavior?
fields.Aliases:
multi-level feedback queue
multilevel feedback queue
fields.Hint: Jobs that use their whole time slice move down.
fields.Fact: OSTEP credits Corbató et al. with first describing it in 1962 for CTSS.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)

fields.Text: MLFQ periodically performs a {{c1::priority boost}}, moving every job to the topmost queue.
fields.Extra: This prevents starvation of long running jobs and adapts to jobs that become interactive.
fields.Hint: It is a periodic reset of priorities.
fields.Fact: OSTEP calls the boost interval a voodoo constant because it is hard to choose well.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)

fields.Question: Which scheduler became Linux's default for normal tasks in version 2.6.23?
fields.Hint: It was written by Ingo Molnar.
fields.Fact: Its documentation says it models an ideal, precise multitasking CPU on real hardware.

fields.Question: Which scheduling algorithm replaced CFS's task selection in Linux 6.6?
fields.Hint: It adds the idea of a virtual deadline.
fields.Fact: The algorithm comes from a 1995 paper by Ion Stoica and Hussein Abdel-Wahab.

fields.Text: CFS runs the task with the smallest {{c1::vruntime}} (virtual runtime).
fields.Extra: Virtual runtime grows more slowly for higher weight tasks.
fields.Hint: It is time spent running, scaled by the task's weight.
fields.Fact: Niceness changes a task's weight, which changes how fast its virtual runtime increases.

fields.Text: CFS keeps runnable tasks in a {{c1::red-black tree}} ordered by virtual runtime.
fields.Extra: The leftmost node is the next task to run.
fields.Hint: It is a self-balancing binary search tree.
fields.Fact: Inserting and removing tasks in this tree takes O(log n) time.

fields.Question: Which Linux real-time scheduling policy is like SCHED_FIFO but with time slices?
fields.Hint: The suffix names a classic policy.
fields.Fact: Real-time policies use static priorities from 1 to 99 on Linux.

fields.Question: Which Linux real-time policy runs a task until it blocks, yields or is preempted by a higher priority task?
fields.Hint: It has no time slicing.
fields.Fact: A runaway task under this policy can starve normal tasks, which is why Linux has real-time throttling.

fields.Question: What is the name of Linux's default time-sharing scheduling policy?
fields.Hint: Inside the kernel it has a different alias.
fields.Fact: Its nice values range from -20 to 19.

fields.Text: On Linux, the nice value ranges from {{c1::-20}} (highest priority) to {{c2::19}} (lowest priority).
fields.Extra: Only privileged processes can lower their nice value.
fields.Hint: A nicer process lets others go first.
fields.Fact: The nice value only affects non real-time policies such as SCHED_OTHER.

fields.Text: {{c1::Lottery}} scheduling gives each job tickets and picks a random winner, so CPU share is proportional to tickets held.
fields.Extra: It is a proportional share scheduler.
fields.Hint: Think of a raffle.
fields.Fact: It was described by Carl Waldspurger and William Weihl in 1994.

fields.Text: {{c1::Stride}} scheduling is a deterministic proportional share scheduler that runs the job with the lowest pass value.
fields.Extra: Each job's pass value advances by its stride, which is inversely proportional to its tickets.
fields.Hint: It is a deterministic cousin of lottery scheduling.
fields.Fact: Unlike lottery scheduling, it needs global state, which makes adding new jobs harder.

fields.Text: Turnaround time is the completion time minus the {{c1::arrival time}}.
fields.Extra: It is a performance metric rather than a fairness metric.
fields.Hint: When did the job show up?
fields.Fact: Optimizing turnaround and response time usually pulls a scheduler in opposite directions.

fields.Text: Response time is the time a job first runs minus its {{c1::arrival time}}.
fields.Extra: Interactive users care most about this metric.
fields.Hint: It measures how quickly the job starts.
fields.Fact: Round robin minimizes response time well but gives poor turnaround.

fields.Question: Which hardware mechanism lets the OS regain the CPU from a process that never yields?
fields.Hint: It fires periodically regardless of what the process does.
fields.Fact: Starting the timer is a privileged operation, so user code cannot disable it.

fields.Text: {{c1::Starvation}} is when a runnable task never gets the CPU because others always take priority.
fields.Extra: Aging or priority boosts are common fixes.
fields.Hint: The task goes hungry.
fields.Fact: Basic MLFQ without boosting can starve long running jobs when many interactive jobs exist.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)

fields.Text: To avoid priority inversion, a lock holder can temporarily run at the waiter's priority, which is called {{c1::priority inheritance}}.
fields.Extra: The low priority holder finishes its critical section sooner.
fields.Hint: The holder borrows a higher priority.
fields.Fact: NASA's 1997 Mars Pathfinder lander suffered resets from priority inversion until priority inheritance was enabled.

fields.Text: {{c1::CPU affinity}} restricts which CPUs a thread may run on; Linux sets it with sched_setaffinity().
fields.Extra: Pinning can improve cache locality.
fields.Hint: Think of a preference for a particular processor.
fields.Fact: The taskset command is a common front end for this setting.

fields.Text: Switching between processes also switches the {{c1::page table}}, which can force TLB entries to be flushed unless they are tagged.
fields.Extra: Threads of the same process avoid this cost.
fields.Hint: It is the structure that maps virtual pages to frames.
fields.Fact: On x86, the page table base address is held in the CR3 register.

fields.Hint: A classic priority-based scheduler.
fields.Fact: Variants of it have been used in BSD Unix, Solaris and Windows NT according to OSTEP.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)

fields.Hint: Linux's former default scheduler.
fields.Fact: It replaced the earlier O(1) scheduler.

fields.Hint: The current Linux scheduler algorithm.
fields.Fact: It considers both a task's lag and its virtual deadline.

fields.Text: A {{c1::system call}} is a controlled entry from user mode into the kernel to request a service.
fields.Extra: The kernel chooses the handler, not the caller.
fields.Hint: read() and write() are examples.
fields.Fact: OSTEP explains that system calls look like ordinary procedure calls because the C library wraps a trap instruction.

fields.Text: CPUs separate {{c1::user mode}} from {{c2::kernel mode}}, and privileged instructions run only in the latter.
fields.Extra: Attempting a privileged instruction in user mode raises an exception.
fields.Hint: One mode is restricted, the other is not.
fields.Fact: x86 calls these privilege levels rings, with the kernel in ring 0 and applications in ring 3.

fields.Question: Which x86-64 instruction do Linux programs use to enter the kernel for a system call?
fields.Hint: It replaced int 0x80 as the fast 64-bit entry path.
fields.Fact: The older int 0x80 path is the 32-bit system call entry.

fields.Text: On x86-64 Linux, the system call number is passed in register {{c1::rax}}.
fields.Extra: Arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9.
fields.Hint: It is also where the return value comes back.
fields.Fact: The fourth argument uses r10 instead of rcx because the syscall instruction overwrites rcx.

fields.Question: In OSTEP, what does the kernel set up at boot to tell hardware where its trap handlers are?
fields.Aliases:
trap tables
interrupt vector table
IDT
interrupt descriptor table
fields.Hint: It is configured by a privileged instruction.
fields.Fact: On x86 this is the interrupt descriptor table, loaded with the lidt instruction.

fields.Text: Most libc system call wrappers return -1 on failure and store the error code in {{c1::errno}}.
fields.Extra: Its value is only meaningful right after a call reports failure.
fields.Hint: Check it only after the call reports failure.
fields.Fact: errno is thread-local, so one thread's failure does not overwrite another's error code.

fields.Question: Which Linux tool prints the system calls a process makes?
fields.Hint: Its output lists each call with its arguments and return value.
fields.Fact: strace is built on the ptrace() system call.

fields.Text: The {{c1::vDSO}} lets calls such as clock_gettime() run in user space without entering the kernel.
fields.Extra: The kernel maps it into every process automatically.
fields.Hint: A small shared library the kernel provides.
fields.Fact: Its name stands for virtual dynamic shared object.

fields.Question:
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
What does read() return at end of file?
fields.Hint: Errors are reported with a different value.
fields.Fact: read() may return fewer bytes than requested even when the file has more data.

fields.Question: Which system call returns the process ID of the caller?
fields.Hint: Its name is a verb plus an abbreviation.
fields.Fact: getppid() returns the parent's process ID instead.

fields.Question: Which system call moves the program break to grow or shrink the heap?
fields.Hint: Classic malloc implementations used it to get memory.
fields.Fact: The program break marks the end of the process's data segment.

fields.Question: Which system call releases a file descriptor?
fields.Hint: Leaking descriptors eventually makes open() fail.
fields.Fact: Closing a descriptor releases any POSIX record locks the process holds on that file.

fields.Question: Which call makes a descriptor a copy of another at a chosen number, as shells do for redirection?
fields.Hint: It is a numbered variant of a shorter call.
fields.Fact: If the target descriptor is already open, it is closed first, atomically.

fields.Text: File descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are standard {{c1::input}}, standard {{c2::output}} and standard {{c3::error}}.
fields.Extra: Programs inherit them from their parent.
fields.Hint: Think of the shell redirections <, > and 2>.
fields.Fact: stderr is typically unbuffered in C so error messages appear immediately.

fields.Text: The {{c1::mmap}}() system call maps files or anonymous memory into a process's address space.
fields.Extra: munmap() removes the mapping.
fields.Hint: Its name is short for memory map.
fields.Fact: With MAP_SHARED, writes to a file mapping are visible to other processes that map the same file.

fields.Text: An {{c1::interrupt}} is an asynchronous signal from hardware, such as a device or timer, that diverts the CPU to a kernel handler.
fields.Extra: System calls, in contrast, are requested synchronously by the program.
fields.Hint: It arrives at a time the program did not choose.
fields.Fact: OSTEP describes interrupts as a way to overlap CPU work with I/O instead of polling.

fields.Question: Which system call returns a new file descriptor for a path?
fields.Hint: Its flags include O_RDONLY and O_CREAT.
fields.Fact: open() returns the lowest numbered descriptor not currently open in the process.

fields.Hint: An IEEE family of standards.
fields.Fact: Richard Stallman suggested the name POSIX to the IEEE committee.

fields.Text: Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of its own private {{c1::address space}}.
fields.Extra: The OS and hardware translate each access to a physical location.
fields.Hint: It is the range of addresses a program can use.
fields.Fact: OSTEP lists transparency, efficiency and protection as the goals of virtual memory.

fields.Hint: Hardware that translates addresses.
fields.Fact: Address translation by the MMU happens on every memory access a program makes.

fields.Text: Paging splits virtual memory into fixed-size {{c1::pages}} and physical memory into page {{c2::frames}}.
fields.Extra: Any page can be placed in any frame.
fields.Hint: Fixed-size units avoid external fragmentation.
fields.Fact: Because all pieces have the same size, paging does not suffer from external fragmentation.

fields.Question: What is the most common base page size on x86-64?
fields.Hint: It is a power of two in kilobytes.
fields.Fact: macOS on Apple silicon uses a larger 16 KiB base page size.

fields.Question: With 4 KiB pages, how many low bits of a virtual address form the page offset?
fields.Hint: Think of the power of two that equals 4096.
fields.Fact: The offset is copied unchanged into the physical address.

fields.Text: A virtual address is split into a virtual page number and an {{c1::offset}}, which is not translated.
fields.Extra: Only the page number is looked up in the page table.
fields.Hint: It locates a byte within the page.
fields.Fact: OSTEP abbreviates the virtual page number as VPN and the physical frame number as PFN.

fields.Hint: A small hardware cache in the MMU.
fields.Fact: A program that touches more pages than the TLB can cover runs noticeably slower.

fields.Text: On a TLB {{c1::miss}}, the translation must be found by walking the page table, which x86 hardware does itself.
fields.Extra: Some architectures, such as MIPS, leave this to software.
fields.Hint: The translation was not cached.
fields.Fact: Software-managed TLBs let the OS use any page table structure it likes.

fields.Text: Some TLBs tag entries with an {{c1::ASID}} so they need not be flushed on every context switch.
fields.Extra: The tag tells which address space an entry belongs to.
fields.Hint: The tag is a small number per address space.
fields.Fact: x86-64 calls its version of this tag a PCID, a process-context identifier.

fields.Question: How many virtual address bits does x86-64 translate with 4-level paging?
fields.Hint: 5-level paging raises it to 57.
fields.Fact: Canonical addresses require bits above the translated range to copy the top translated bit.

fields.Text: {{c1::Multi-level}} page tables save memory because table pages for unused regions of the address space need not exist.
fields.Extra: Each level indexes the next, like a tree.
fields.Hint: Think of a tree of tables.
fields.Fact: The cost is extra memory lookups on a TLB miss, one per level.

fields.Hint: One per mapped virtual page.
fields.Fact: x86 PTEs include an NX bit that marks a page as non-executable.

fields.Text: Besides the frame number, a page table entry typically has bits such as {{c1::present}} (or valid), {{c2::dirty}} and accessed.
fields.Extra: The hardware sets the dirty bit when the page is written.
fields.Hint: One bit says whether the page is in memory at all.
fields.Fact: The dirty bit lets the OS skip writing unmodified pages back to disk on eviction.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Paging: Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf)
OSTEP: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-beyondphys.pdf)

fields.Question: What is the event when a program accesses a page that is not currently mapped to a frame?
fields.Hint: The hardware hands control to the OS to fix it up.
fields.Fact: Most page faults are handled transparently and the program never notices.

fields.Text: On Linux, a {{c1::minor}} page fault is resolved without disk I/O, while a {{c2::major}} fault needs to read from storage.
fields.Extra: Both are counted per process, for example by /usr/bin/time -v.
fields.Hint: The two words also describe a scale of importance.
fields.Fact: A minor fault can happen when a page is already in the page cache but not yet mapped by this process.

fields.Text: An access to an unmapped or forbidden address usually delivers {{c1::SIGSEGV}} to the process.
fields.Extra: This is what a segmentation fault is.
fields.Hint: Its name refers to segmentation.
fields.Fact: The default action for this signal is to terminate the process and dump core.

fields.Text: {{c1::Demand paging}} loads a page into memory only when it is first accessed.
fields.Extra: Programs can start before their whole image is in memory.
fields.Hint: Pages arrive when asked for.
fields.Fact: Executables are typically mapped this way, so unused code is never read from disk.

fields.Question: Which page replacement policy evicts the page that has gone unused the longest?
fields.Hint: It uses the recent past to predict the future.
fields.Fact: Exact LRU is expensive, so real systems approximate it with reference bits.

fields.Question: Which theoretical policy evicts the page that will next be used furthest in the future?
fields.Aliases:
optimal
MIN
Belady's MIN
Belady's algorithm
fields.Hint: It is unimplementable but useful as a benchmark.
fields.Fact: It was described by László Bélády in 1966.

fields.Question: Which page replacement policy evicts the page that was loaded earliest, regardless of use?
fields.Hint: It ignores how recently a page was touched.
fields.Fact: This policy can suffer from Belady's anomaly.

fields.Question: Which policy approximates LRU by sweeping a circular list and clearing use bits?
fields.Hint: Picture a hand moving around a circle.
fields.Fact: A page with its use bit set gets a second chance and is skipped once.

fields.Text: {{c1::Belady's anomaly}} is when adding frames increases the number of page faults, as can happen under FIFO.
fields.Extra: LRU and OPT never show it, because they are stack algorithms.
fields.Hint: It is named after a researcher.
fields.Fact: Bélády, Nelson and Shedler published the anomaly in 1969.

fields.Text: {{c1::Thrashing}} is when a system spends most of its time paging because active memory demands exceed physical memory.
fields.Extra: Throughput collapses while the disk is busy.
fields.Hint: The system is busy but makes little progress.
fields.Fact: Linux may respond to severe memory pressure by running the OOM killer.

fields.Text: A process's {{c1::working set}} is the set of pages it has referenced in a recent window of time.
fields.Extra: Keeping it in memory avoids frequent faults.
fields.Hint: Peter Denning introduced the idea.
fields.Fact: Denning proposed the working set model in 1968.

fields.Question: Which Linux kernel mechanism terminates a process when memory is exhausted?
fields.Aliases:
out of memory killer
OOM
oom-killer
fields.Hint: Its name abbreviates the situation it handles.
fields.Fact: Each process's /proc/[pid]/oom_score_adj can make it more or less likely to be chosen.

fields.Text: Linux's vm.overcommit_memory value of {{c1::0}}, the default, uses heuristic overcommit.
fields.Extra: A value of 2 enables strict accounting.
fields.Hint: It is the lowest of the three allowed values.
fields.Fact: With overcommit, malloc() can succeed for memory the system cannot actually back later.

fields.Text: Huge pages on x86-64 are commonly {{c1::2 MiB}} or 1 GiB in size.
fields.Extra: Larger pages increase TLB reach.
fields.Hint: It is 512 times the base page size.
fields.Fact: One 2 MiB huge page covers what would otherwise need 512 TLB entries for 4 KiB pages.
fields.Source: Linux kernel docs: Transparent Hugepage Support (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html)

fields.Text: {{c1::Transparent Huge Pages}} let Linux back memory with huge pages without application changes.
fields.Extra: Applications can also give hints with madvise().
fields.Hint: It works without the program noticing.
fields.Fact: The khugepaged kernel thread collapses ranges of small pages into huge pages in the background.
fields.Source: Linux kernel docs: Transparent Hugepage Support (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html)

fields.Hint: A security hardening technique.
fields.Fact: Linux controls it with /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space.

fields.Text: {{c1::Swap space}} on disk holds pages evicted from physical memory.
fields.Extra: Swapped pages are read back on a major fault.
fields.Hint: It is space reserved for moving pages out.
fields.Fact: OSTEP notes that the present bit tells the hardware whether a page is in memory or swapped out.

fields.Text: {{c1::External fragmentation}} is free memory split into pieces too small to satisfy a request.
fields.Extra: Coalescing adjacent free blocks reduces it.
fields.Hint: The waste is outside allocated blocks.
fields.Fact: Variable-sized allocation schemes, such as segmentation, suffer from it.

fields.Text: {{c1::Internal fragmentation}} is wasted space inside an allocated block that is larger than requested.
fields.Extra: Rounding to fixed sizes causes it.
fields.Hint: The waste is inside allocated blocks.
fields.Fact: Paging trades external fragmentation for internal fragmentation in the last page.

fields.Question: Which allocation strategy picks the smallest free block that is large enough?
fields.Hint: It tries to waste as little as possible per request.
fields.Fact: It must search the whole free list unless the list is sorted.

fields.Question: Which allocation strategy takes the first free block that is large enough?
fields.Hint: It stops searching early.
fields.Fact: It tends to leave small fragments near the start of the free list.

fields.Question: Which allocation strategy picks the largest free block?
fields.Hint: It aims to leave large remainders.
fields.Fact: OSTEP reports that studies show it usually performs badly.

fields.Question: Which variant of first fit resumes searching where the previous search ended?
fields.Hint: It keeps a pointer into the free list.
fields.Fact: It spreads searches more evenly through the list.

fields.Text: A {{c1::buddy}} allocator splits memory into power-of-two blocks and merges a freed block with its neighbor when both are free.
fields.Extra: Linux's page allocator uses this scheme.
fields.Hint: Each block has a partner of the same size.
fields.Fact: Finding a block's partner is cheap because their addresses differ in a single bit.

fields.Text: A {{c1::slab}} allocator keeps caches of same-size kernel objects so they can be reused quickly.
fields.Extra: It reduces fragmentation and initialization cost.
fields.Hint: It was introduced by Jeff Bonwick for Solaris.
fields.Fact: Linux today uses the SLUB implementation of this design.

fields.Text: glibc malloc() serves large requests with {{c1::mmap}} instead of the heap.
fields.Extra: The default threshold is 128 KiB and adjusts dynamically.
fields.Hint: It is the same call used to map files.
fields.Fact: Memory from such allocations goes straight back to the OS when freed.

fields.Question:
char *p = malloc(16);
free(p);
free(p);
What bug does this code contain?
fields.Hint: Count how many times the memory is released.
fields.Fact: This is undefined behavior and can corrupt the allocator's internal data.

fields.Question:
char *p = malloc(16);
free(p);
p[0] = 'x';
What bug does this code contain?
fields.Hint: Look at what happens after the memory is released.
fields.Fact: OSTEP calls a pointer to freed memory a dangling pointer.

fields.Question: What is the bug called when a program allocates memory and never frees it after it is no longer needed?
fields.Hint: Long-running programs suffer most.
fields.Fact: Memory still in use when a process exits is reclaimed by the OS anyway.

fields.Text: A {{c1::race condition}} is when the result depends on the timing of concurrent accesses to shared data.
fields.Extra: Incrementing a shared counter from two threads is the classic example.
fields.Hint: Two threads compete to get there first.
fields.Fact: A data race specifically means unsynchronized concurrent accesses where at least one is a write.

fields.Text: A {{c1::critical section}} is code that accesses a shared resource and must not run in more than one thread at a time.
fields.Extra: Locks surround it.
fields.Hint: It is the part that needs protection.
fields.Fact: OSTEP uses the term mutual exclusion for guaranteeing only one thread is inside.

fields.Question: Which primitive provides mutual exclusion through lock and unlock operations by its owner?
fields.Hint: Its name is a contraction.
fields.Fact: glibc builds its pthread mutexes on Linux futexes.

fields.Question: Which primitive is an integer with wait and post operations?
fields.Hint: Wait decrements and may block; post increments.
fields.Fact: Dijkstra introduced this primitive in the 1960s.

fields.Question: Which primitive lets a thread sleep, with a mutex held, until another thread signals that a condition may be true?
fields.Hint: It always works together with a mutex.
fields.Fact: Signaling it when no thread is waiting has no lasting effect, unlike a semaphore post.

fields.Question: Which lock lets many readers in at once, or a single writer?
fields.Hint: It suits data that is read far more often than written.
fields.Fact: Simple implementations can starve writers if readers keep arriving.

fields.Question: Which kind of lock busy waits in a loop until it becomes free?
fields.Hint: It never puts the thread to sleep.
fields.Fact: Spinning wastes CPU on a single processor, since the holder cannot run while the waiter spins.

fields.Text: Dijkstra named the two semaphore operations {{c1::P}} and {{c2::V}}.
fields.Extra: They correspond to wait and post.
fields.Hint: Both are single letters taken from Dutch words.
fields.Fact: Dijkstra was Dutch, which is why the operation names come from Dutch.

fields.Text: A semaphore initialized to {{c1::1}} can be used as a lock.
fields.Extra: This is called a binary semaphore.
fields.Hint: Only one thread should be able to pass.
fields.Fact: OSTEP shows that a semaphore initialized to 0 can be used for ordering instead.

fields.Question:
pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
while (!ready)
    pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m);
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
Why is the condition checked in a while loop instead of an if?
fields.Aliases:
spurious wakeup
the condition may be false on wakeup
fields.Hint: Waking up does not prove the condition holds.
fields.Fact: Another thread may also consume the state between the signal and the wakeup, so rechecking is always required.
fields.Source: pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Text: pthread_cond_wait() atomically {{c1::releases the mutex}} and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning.
fields.Extra: This prevents a lost wakeup between checking and sleeping.
fields.Hint: Think about what must happen to the lock while sleeping.
fields.Fact: Calling it without holding the mutex is undefined behavior.
fields.Source: pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Question: Which atomic instruction writes a new value only if the current value equals an expected one?
fields.Aliases:
CAS
compare and swap
compare-and-exchange
cmpxchg
fields.Hint: x86 implements it as cmpxchg.
fields.Fact: It is the building block of most lock-free data structures.

fields.Question: Which atomic instruction sets a memory location and returns its old value, used for simple spinlocks?
fields.Hint: Its name describes both steps.
fields.Fact: OSTEP builds its first working spinlock from this instruction.

fields.Question: Which atomic instruction increments a value and returns the old one, used to build ticket locks?
fields.Aliases:
fetch and add
atomic add
xadd
fields.Hint: Ticket locks hand out numbers with it.
fields.Fact: Ticket locks built this way serve threads in order, so they guarantee progress for every waiter.

fields.Text: A Linux {{c1::futex}} lets an uncontended lock be taken entirely in user space, entering the kernel only to wait or wake.
fields.Extra: glibc builds pthread mutexes on it.
fields.Hint: Its name is a contraction that describes speed.
fields.Fact: Futexes first appeared in a stable kernel with Linux 2.6.0.

fields.Text: {{c1::Peterson's}} algorithm achieves mutual exclusion for two threads using only loads and stores.
fields.Extra: It assumes memory operations are not reordered.
fields.Hint: It is named after its author, published in 1981.
fields.Fact: On modern CPUs with relaxed memory ordering it needs memory fences to work.

fields.Text: OSTEP's bounded buffer uses semaphores named {{c1::empty}} and {{c2::full}}, plus a mutex.
fields.Extra: One counts free slots and the other counts filled slots.
fields.Hint: The names describe slot states.
fields.Fact: The mutex must be acquired inside the semaphore waits, or the code can deadlock.

fields.Text: A {{c1::memory barrier}} restricts how the CPU and compiler reorder memory operations around it.
fields.Extra: Lock implementations include them.
fields.Hint: It is also called a fence.
fields.Fact: x86 provides mfence, while ARM uses dmb.

fields.Text: OSTEP finds that most non-deadlock concurrency bugs are {{c1::atomicity violation}} or order violation bugs.
fields.Extra: One assumes code runs as a unit; the other assumes an order.
fields.Hint: A sequence was assumed to happen without interruption.
fields.Fact: The study OSTEP cites, by Lu et al. in 2008, examined bugs in MySQL, Apache, Mozilla and OpenOffice.

fields.Text: Deadlock requires {{c1::mutual exclusion}}, {{c2::hold and wait}}, {{c3::no preemption}} and {{c4::circular wait}}.
fields.Extra: Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.
fields.Hint: Four conditions in total.
fields.Fact: These are often called the Coffman conditions, after a 1971 survey paper.
fields.Source:
Coffman, Elphick, Shoshani: System Deadlocks (ACM Computing Surveys, 1971) (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/356586.356588)
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: Which deadlock condition is broken by always acquiring locks in one global order?
fields.Hint: A cycle in the wait graph becomes impossible.
fields.Fact: OSTEP points to Linux memory mapping code whose comments list the required lock acquisition orders.

fields.Question: Which deadlock condition is broken by acquiring all needed locks at once, atomically?
fields.Hint: Threads never hold one resource while waiting for another.
fields.Fact: OSTEP notes this approach reduces concurrency, since locks are taken early.

fields.Question: Which deadlock condition does pthread_mutex_trylock() help break, by letting a thread back off and release what it holds?
fields.Hint: Resources are normally not forcibly taken away.
fields.Fact: Backing off and retrying can cause livelock instead.

fields.Question: Which deadlock condition do lock-free data structures avoid?
fields.Hint: They rely on atomic hardware instructions instead of locks.
fields.Fact: OSTEP builds such structures from compare-and-swap.

fields.Text: Dijkstra's {{c1::banker's algorithm}} avoids deadlock by granting only requests that keep the system in a safe state.
fields.Extra: It needs each process's maximum demand in advance.
fields.Hint: It is named after a lender with limited cash.
fields.Fact: Because maximum demands are rarely known, general purpose OSes seldom use it.

fields.Text: {{c1::Livelock}} is when threads keep reacting to each other and change state, but none makes progress.
fields.Extra: Random backoff before retrying helps.
fields.Hint: Busy rather than blocked.
fields.Fact: Unlike deadlocked threads, livelocked threads consume CPU time.

fields.Text: Deadlock detection often searches a {{c1::wait-for graph}} for cycles.
fields.Extra: Each edge means one task waits for another.
fields.Hint: A graph of who waits on whom.
fields.Fact: Many database systems detect deadlocks this way and abort one transaction.

fields.Question: Who first posed the problem now known as the dining philosophers?
fields.Hint: He also invented semaphores.
fields.Fact: Tony Hoare later gave the problem its familiar dining philosophers form.

fields.Question:
// thread 1
lock(&a); lock(&b);
// thread 2
lock(&b); lock(&a);
What can happen when these threads run concurrently?
fields.Hint: Each thread may end up holding what the other wants.
fields.Fact: Acquiring a and b in the same order in both threads removes the problem.

fields.Text: The Linux kernel's {{c1::lockdep}} validator reports lock ordering problems that could deadlock, even if no deadlock has happened yet.
fields.Extra: It tracks the order in which lock classes are acquired.
fields.Hint: The validator is enabled with CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING.
fields.Fact: It works by learning ordering from every run rather than waiting for an actual hang.
fields.Source: Linux kernel docs: Runtime locking correctness validator (https://docs.kernel.org/locking/lockdep-design.html)

fields.Text: An {{c1::inode}} stores a file's metadata and the location of its data, but not its name.
fields.Extra: Names live elsewhere.
fields.Hint: ls -i prints its number.
fields.Fact: Running out of inodes can stop new files being created even when disk space remains.
fields.Source:
inode(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inode.7.html)
OSTEP: File System Implementation (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-implementation.pdf)

fields.Question: Where is a file's name stored in a Unix file system?
fields.Aliases:
directory
dentry
in the directory
parent directory
fields.Hint: The inode does not hold it.
fields.Fact: Linux caches name lookups in the dentry cache.

fields.Text: A {{c1::hard link}} is an additional directory entry that refers to the same inode.
fields.Extra: Deleting one name leaves the file reachable by the other.
fields.Hint: Created with ln without options.
fields.Fact: Most systems forbid hard links to directories to keep the tree acyclic.

fields.Text: A {{c1::symbolic link}} is a file that stores a path to another file and can dangle if the target is removed.
fields.Extra: It can point across file systems.
fields.Hint: Created with ln -s.
fields.Fact: Its length is the length of the stored path, not of the target file.

fields.Question: Which system call removes a name from the file system?
fields.Hint: rm uses it.
fields.Fact: The file's data is freed only when its link count is zero and no process has it open.

fields.Question: Which field of struct stat counts a file's hard links?
fields.Hint: Its prefix is shared by every field of the struct.
fields.Fact: A new directory has a link count of 2: its name in the parent and its own . entry.

fields.Question: Which system call returns a file's metadata, such as size and owner?
fields.Hint: The shell command has the same name.
fields.Fact: lstat() reports on a symbolic link itself instead of following it.

fields.Question: Which ls option prints each file's inode number?
fields.Hint: The option is a single lowercase letter.
fields.Fact: Two hard links to the same file show the same inode number.

fields.Text: Hard links cannot span file systems because inode numbers are only unique within a single {{c1::file system}}.
fields.Extra: Symbolic links have no such limit.
fields.Hint: Each mounted volume numbers its own inodes.
fields.Fact: link() fails with EXDEV when the paths are on different mounted file systems.

fields.Text: {{c1::Journaling}} file systems write intended updates to a log first, so they can recover consistently after a crash.
fields.Extra: It replaces a full fsck scan with a short log replay.
fields.Hint: Also called write-ahead logging.
fields.Fact: OSTEP describes how ext3 added journaling on top of the ext2 layout.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-journaling.pdf)

fields.Text: ext4's default data mode is {{c1::ordered}}, which journals metadata and writes data blocks before their metadata is committed.
fields.Extra: The other modes are journal and writeback.
fields.Hint: The mode name describes a write ordering.
fields.Fact: OSTEP calls this approach metadata journaling.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: ext4 General Information (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/ext4.html)
OSTEP: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-journaling.pdf)

fields.Question: Which Unix tool scans a file system to find and repair inconsistencies after a crash?
fields.Hint: It is usually run at boot after an unclean shutdown.
fields.Fact: OSTEP notes its main problem is that it is too slow for large disks.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-journaling.pdf)

fields.Aliases:
virtual filesystem
virtual file system switch
fields.Hint: The kernel layer above concrete file systems.
fields.Fact: Through it, the same read() works on ext4, NFS and /proc.
fields.Source: Linux kernel docs: Overview of the Linux Virtual File System (https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/vfs.html)

fields.Hint: A small integer.
fields.Fact: It indexes the process's table of open files.

fields.Question: Classic Unix inodes use direct pointers plus single, double and which other indirect pointer?
fields.Aliases:
triple
triple indirect pointer
triple indirect block
fields.Hint: Count one level more.
fields.Fact: Indirect pointers let small files stay cheap while still allowing very large files.

fields.Text: ext4 records file data with {{c1::extents}}, each a starting block and a length, instead of one pointer per block.
fields.Extra: Large contiguous files need very little metadata.
fields.Hint: A contiguous run of blocks.
fields.Fact: With 4 KiB blocks, a single ext4 extent can cover up to 128 MiB of contiguous data.
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: ext4 General Information (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/ext4.html)
OSTEP: File System Implementation (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-implementation.pdf)

fields.Text: {{c1::fsync}}() blocks until a file's modified data and metadata have been passed to the storage device.
fields.Extra: Without it, write() may only reach the page cache.
fields.Hint: Databases call it before acknowledging a commit.
fields.Fact: To make a new file's name durable, the containing directory may also need to be synced.

fields.Text: The {{c1::page cache}} keeps file data in RAM so repeated reads avoid disk I/O.
fields.Extra: Writes are usually buffered here and flushed later.
fields.Hint: It caches pages of files.
fields.Fact: free on Linux reports this memory as buff/cache, and it can be reclaimed when needed.

fields.Text: A directory's contents map file names to {{c1::inode numbers}}.
fields.Extra: Path lookup reads these mappings one component at a time.
fields.Hint: What identifies a file inside the file system?
fields.Fact: Path resolution starts at / for absolute paths and the current directory for relative ones.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Interlude: Files and Directories (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-intro.pdf)
path_resolution(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/path_resolution.7.html)

fields.Question: What does the execute permission bit allow on a directory?
fields.Hint: It is not about running a program.
fields.Fact: Without it, a path through the directory cannot be resolved even if names can be listed.

fields.Text: The {{c1::superblock}} holds information about the whole file system, such as its size and number of inodes.
fields.Extra: It is read at mount time.
fields.Hint: It sits above the other metadata.
fields.Fact: ext file systems store backup copies of it in several block groups.

fields.Text: Simple file systems such as OSTEP's vsfs track free inodes and data blocks with {{c1::bitmaps}}.
fields.Extra: Each bit marks one item as used or free.
fields.Hint: One bit per item.
fields.Fact: OSTEP's crash examples show bitmaps and inodes getting out of sync after a crash.

fields.Question: In which I/O model does read() put the thread to sleep until data is ready?
fields.Hint: It is the default for file descriptors.
fields.Fact: A thread-per-connection server relies on this model.

fields.Question: Which I/O model makes read() fail immediately instead of waiting when no data is ready?
fields.Hint: It is enabled with a flag on the descriptor.
fields.Fact: It is usually paired with a readiness API so the program knows when to retry.

fields.Question: Which open() flag makes I/O on a descriptor non-blocking?
fields.Hint: It can also be set later with fcntl().
fields.Fact: For regular files on Linux, this flag has no effect on reads and writes.

fields.Question: Which errno does a non-blocking read return when no data is available?
fields.Hint: It suggests trying once more.
fields.Fact: On Linux the two names for this error have the same value.

fields.Question: Which Linux API monitors many file descriptors for readiness and scales well to large numbers of them?
fields.Hint: It was added in the Linux 2.5 development series.
fields.Fact: Unlike poll(), the interest list stays in the kernel between calls.

fields.Question: Which event notification API do FreeBSD and macOS provide in place of epoll?
fields.Hint: Events are submitted and returned with kevent().
fields.Fact: kqueue first appeared in FreeBSD 4.1.

fields.Question: Which POSIX call takes an array of pollfd structures to wait on several descriptors?
fields.Hint: It is named after the act of checking.
fields.Fact: It avoids select()'s fixed descriptor limit, but still scans every entry on each call.

fields.Text: In {{c1::edge-triggered}} mode (EPOLLET), epoll reports only changes in readiness, so the program should read until EAGAIN.
fields.Extra: Stopping early can leave data unreported.
fields.Hint: Think of a signal's rising edge.
fields.Fact: The epoll man page recommends non-blocking descriptors with this mode.

fields.Text: epoll's default mode is {{c1::level-triggered}}, which reports a descriptor as long as it remains ready.
fields.Extra: It behaves like a faster poll().
fields.Hint: It is the opposite of edge-triggered.
fields.Fact: Level-triggered mode is more forgiving if a program does not drain a socket completely.

fields.Text: An epoll program creates an instance with {{c1::epoll_create1}}(), registers descriptors with {{c2::epoll_ctl}}(), and waits with {{c3::epoll_wait}}().
fields.Extra: The instance itself is a file descriptor.
fields.Hint: All three start with the same prefix.
fields.Fact: Because the epoll instance is a descriptor, it can be nested inside another epoll instance.

fields.Text: select() can only handle descriptor numbers below FD_SETSIZE, which is {{c1::1024}} on Linux.
fields.Extra: Higher descriptors cause undefined behavior.
fields.Hint: It is a power of two.
fields.Fact: The select man page recommends poll() or epoll for modern applications for this reason.

fields.Question: In which Linux kernel version was io_uring introduced?
fields.Hint: It arrived in 2019.
fields.Fact: io_uring was created by Jens Axboe.

fields.Text: io_uring shares two ring buffers with the kernel: the {{c1::submission queue}} and the {{c2::completion queue}}.
fields.Extra: Applications write requests to one and read results from the other.
fields.Hint: One ring goes in each direction.
fields.Fact: Sharing the rings in memory lets many operations be submitted with a single system call, or none.

fields.Text: io_uring is a {{c1::completion}}-based interface: operations are submitted and their results collected later, unlike epoll's readiness model.
fields.Extra: The kernel performs the I/O itself.
fields.Hint: The program learns when work is done, not when it could start.
fields.Fact: Unlike epoll, io_uring can perform reads and writes on regular files asynchronously.

fields.Question: Which system call tells the kernel to consume io_uring submissions and optionally wait for completions?
fields.Hint: It is one of the three io_uring syscalls.
fields.Fact: The other two are io_uring_setup() and io_uring_register().

fields.Question: Which system call creates an io_uring instance?
fields.Hint: It returns a file descriptor for the instance.
fields.Fact: The rings are then mapped into the process with mmap().

fields.Question: Which library provides helpers that hide io_uring's raw ring setup?
fields.Hint: It is maintained alongside the kernel interface.
fields.Fact: Its helpers include io_uring_queue_init() and io_uring_get_sqe().

fields.Text: With IORING_SETUP_{{c1::SQPOLL}}, a kernel thread polls the submission queue so the program can submit without system calls.
fields.Extra: The thread sleeps after an idle period.
fields.Hint: The flag is passed to io_uring_setup().
fields.Fact: This trades a busy kernel thread for lower submission latency.

fields.Hint: One io_uring request.
fields.Fact: Each entry names an operation, such as a read, and its arguments.

fields.Hint: One io_uring result.
fields.Fact: Each carries the user_data value from its request, so results can be matched to requests.

fields.Hint: Devices copy data without the CPU.
fields.Fact: The CPU is notified with an interrupt when the transfer is done.

fields.Text: For very fast devices, {{c1::polling}} can outperform interrupts by avoiding interrupt handling overhead.
fields.Extra: Hybrid approaches poll briefly, then fall back to interrupts.
fields.Hint: Repeatedly checking a status register.
fields.Fact: OSTEP warns that interrupts can cause livelock under a flood of network packets.

fields.Text: Opening a file with O_DIRECT tries to bypass the {{c1::page cache}}.
fields.Extra: Buffers often need specific alignment.
fields.Hint: The kernel's cache for file data.
fields.Fact: Databases use it because they manage their own caching.

fields.Question: Which Linux call copies data between descriptors inside the kernel, often to send a file to a socket?
fields.Hint: It avoids copying through a user space buffer.
fields.Fact: Because data stays in the kernel, no user space buffer is needed for the copy.

fields.Question: Which signal terminates a process and cannot be caught, blocked or ignored?
fields.Hint: It is a last resort.
fields.Fact: The only other signal that cannot be caught, blocked or ignored is SIGSTOP.

fields.Question: Which signal stops a process and cannot be caught, blocked or ignored?
fields.Hint: The process can later be resumed.
fields.Fact: SIGTSTP, sent by Ctrl+Z, is the catchable version.

fields.Question: Which signal does the kill command send by default?
fields.Hint: It politely asks a process to exit.
fields.Fact: Its number is 15.

fields.Question: Which signal does pressing Ctrl+C in a terminal send to the foreground process group?
fields.Hint: It is the usual way to cancel a running command.
fields.Fact: Its default action is to terminate the process.

fields.Question: Which signal does a parent receive when a child terminates or stops?
fields.Hint: Shells rely on it to notice finished background jobs.
fields.Fact: Setting its action to SIG_IGN makes Linux reap children automatically, so no zombies form.

fields.Question: Which signal is sent when writing to a pipe with no readers?
fields.Hint: It is named after the channel involved.
fields.Fact: If the signal is ignored, write() fails with EPIPE instead.

fields.Question: Which signal resumes a stopped process?
fields.Hint: Shells send it when you run fg or bg.
fields.Fact: It is the only signal that resumes a process stopped by SIGSTOP.

fields.Question: What is the signal number of SIGKILL?
fields.Hint: It is the famous number in kill -9.
fields.Fact: SIGKILL has the value 9 on every common architecture, unlike some other signals.

fields.Text: {{c1::sigaction}}() is the preferred way to install signal handlers, because signal() behaves differently across systems.
fields.Extra: It lets you set flags such as SA_RESTART.
fields.Hint: It takes a struct of the same name as an argument.
fields.Fact: SA_RESTART makes some interrupted system calls restart instead of failing with EINTR.

fields.Text: A signal handler may only safely call {{c1::async-signal-safe}} functions, and printf() is not one of them.
fields.Extra: write() is on the list.
fields.Hint: The rule is about functions safe to call asynchronously.
fields.Fact: The signal-safety man page lists the functions POSIX requires to be safe.

fields.Question: Which system call changes the set of signals blocked by a single-threaded process?
fields.Hint: Multithreaded programs use a pthread variant.
fields.Fact: Blocked signals stay pending until they are unblocked.

fields.Text: Linux containers are built mainly from {{c1::namespaces}} for isolation and {{c2::cgroups}} for resource control.
fields.Extra: Neither feature was designed only for containers.
fields.Hint: One limits what a process sees, the other how much it uses.
fields.Fact: There is no single container object in the Linux kernel.
fields.Source:
namespaces(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html)
cgroups(7), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/cgroups.7.html)

fields.Question: Which namespace gives processes their own process ID numbering?
fields.Hint: Inside, the first process gets ID 1.
fields.Fact: A process can see processes in its own and descendant PID namespaces, but not in its ancestors.

fields.Question: Which namespace isolates the list of mount points a process sees?
fields.Hint: It was the first namespace Linux added.
fields.Fact: Its clone flag is CLONE_NEWNS, a name chosen when it was the only namespace type.

fields.Question: Which namespace gives a process its own network devices, addresses and routing tables?
fields.Hint: The ip netns command manages them.
fields.Fact: A virtual Ethernet (veth) pair is commonly used to connect two of them.

fields.Question: Which namespace lets a process be root inside it while unprivileged outside?
fields.Hint: It maps user and group IDs.
fields.Fact: Since Linux 3.8, unprivileged processes can create this namespace.

fields.Question: Which namespace isolates the hostname and NIS domain name?
fields.Hint: Its name comes from the uname() structure.
fields.Fact: UTS stands for UNIX Time-sharing System.

fields.Text: The first process created in a new PID namespace has PID {{c1::1}} inside it.
fields.Extra: It acts as init for that namespace.
fields.Hint: Same as init on the host.
fields.Fact: If this process exits, every other process in the namespace is killed.

fields.Hint: Limits CPU, memory and I/O.
fields.Fact: cgroups were merged into Linux 2.6.24.

fields.Hint: It publishes runtime and image specifications.
fields.Fact: It was founded in 2015 under the Linux Foundation.

fields.Text: cgroup {{c1::v2}} organizes all controllers in a single unified hierarchy.
fields.Extra: v1 allowed a separate hierarchy per controller.
fields.Hint: A version number.
fields.Fact: cgroup v2 was declared non-experimental in Linux 4.5.
fields.Source: Linux kernel docs: Control Group v2 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

fields.Text: Containers share the host's {{c1::kernel}}, while virtual machines run their own.
fields.Extra: This is why containers start quickly.
fields.Hint: The core part of the OS.
fields.Fact: A kernel vulnerability can therefore affect every container on a host.

fields.Question: Which system call moves the calling thread into an existing namespace?
fields.Hint: The nsenter command uses it.
fields.Fact: Namespaces are referred to by file descriptors from /proc/[pid]/ns.

fields.Question: Which system call moves the caller into new namespaces without creating a new process?
fields.Hint: A command of the same name exposes it.
fields.Fact: For a new PID namespace, only children created afterward are placed in it.

fields.Text: {{c1::seccomp}} filters restrict which system calls a process may make.
fields.Extra: Filters are written as BPF programs.
fields.Hint: It is configured with prctl() or a system call of the same name.
fields.Fact: Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks some rarely needed system calls.

fields.Text: {{c1::chroot}}() changes a process's root directory for path lookup, but it is not a security boundary on its own.
fields.Extra: Privileged processes can escape it.
fields.Hint: Build environments have used it for decades.
fields.Fact: Its man page notes it does not change the current working directory.

fields.Question: What is the name of the OCI reference container runtime?
fields.Hint: It is a command line tool written in Go.
fields.Fact: Docker donated it to the OCI.

fields.Text: Linux {{c1::capabilities}} divide root's privileges into separate units such as CAP_NET_ADMIN.
fields.Extra: Containers usually run with a reduced set.
fields.Hint: Each unit is named CAP_ something.
fields.Fact: CAP_SYS_ADMIN covers so many operations that it is often described as the new root.
